title: How I use AI across my whole indie pipeline – art, trailers, music and code for a live reaction game
author: thexyba
selftext:
Hey r/aigamedev 👋

I'm a solo dev working on **Scitch**, a live multiplayer reaction game for iPhone & Android (colored balls, a new mini-game every round, slowest players get knocked out). It's in open beta now, and since this sub is about *how* AI is used in game dev, I wanted to share my actual workflow – what worked, what didn't.

**1. Character & avatar art – image generation** All 60+ unlockable avatars and the characters in my trailers are AI-generated (Gemini image model / "Nano Banana Pro"). What made the difference:

* Always passing an existing character as a **style reference**, otherwise every new avatar looks like it's from a different game
* Generating on a flat magenta background and keying it out in Python → clean cutouts I can animate
* For backgrounds I generate one "base" painting and then *edit* it (e.g. summer → Halloween night) instead of generating from scratch, so the composition stays identical

**2. Trailers & social videos – written as code, not edited** I don't use a video editor. Every trailer/short is an HTML page with Web Animations, rendered frame by frame with Playwright and stitched with ffmpeg. An AI coding assistant writes and iterates the animation code with me ("the journal page flip looks fake", "the shop balls leave a ghost when they jump" → fix → re-render). Big upside: everything is deterministic, so EN/DE versions and 9:16 / 16:9 cuts are just a parameter.

**3. Music & sound – synthesized in Python** The trailer tracks (a "summer mystery" theme, a comedy march, an electro-pop loop) are generated with numpy/scipy – no samples, no licensing headaches, and I can make the music hit exactly on scene cuts because the beat grid is shared with the animation timeline.

**4. Game code** Flutter app + Go game server + Laravel backend. AI helps a lot with the boring-but-critical parts (protocol changes across client/server, tests, i18n), but game feel and balancing are still very much manual playtesting.

**What didn't work well**

* Image models love adding extra hands or melting details on small sprites → lots of re-rolls
* Cutting objects out of a painting to animate them (e.g. balls in a shop) needs real cleanup work, otherwise you get halos and leftover shadows
* AI is great at "make it work", much worse at "make it feel good" – that part still needs a human eye

Happy to go deeper on any part (the video-as-code setup is probably the most reusable thing here).

If you want to try the game: the beta is free → scitch.com/beta And I'd genuinely love feedback: does the art style feel consistent, or can you tell it's AI?
